title: The history of the transistor, from 1947 to the first microprocessor
summary: A map of people, labs, and inventions from the point-contact transistor to the first microprocessors — geography and relationships, not a pure timeline.

blocks.eyebrow: B render — map of people, labs, inventions
blocks.title: The transistor as a network, not a stopwatch
blocks.body: From Bell Labs in 1947 to the first microprocessors ~1971, the story is a map: labs that spawn people, people who carry ideas to new buildings, inventions that pull the next lab into existence. Read the nodes and edges; dates are anchors, not the spine.

items.label: Devices and processes that redraw the map

blocks.heading: Lab map — where the work clustered

nodes.title: Bell Telephone Laboratories (Murray Hill / NY metro)
nodes.detail: Point-contact transistor (1947). Shockley, Bardeen, Brattain. Industrial research scale; information theory neighbors semiconductor physics.

nodes.title: Shockley Semiconductor (Mountain View)
nodes.detail: Shockley's West Coast bet. Traitorous Eight leave → Fairchild. Silicon Valley's original fracture line.

nodes.title: Fairchild Semiconductor (Mountain View / Palo Alto orbit)
nodes.detail: Planar process home. Noyce, Moore, and a generation of spinouts. Integrated circuits become manufacturable.

nodes.title: Texas Instruments (Dallas)
nodes.detail: Kilby's integrated circuit demonstration; volume silicon culture parallel to the Bay.

nodes.title: Intel (Mountain View → Santa Clara)
nodes.detail: Fairchild alumni. Memory first, then the microprocessor as a product category.

nodes.title: Other nodes on the edge
nodes.detail: IBM, Japanese labs, military/avionics contractors — customers and co-inventors who pull reliability and packaging forward.

blocks.heading: People map — who carries the spark

nodes.title: Bardeen & Brattain
nodes.detail: Point-contact device demonstration at Bell — physics made tangible.

nodes.title: William Shockley
nodes.detail: Junction transistor theory/leadership; later Shockley Semi — catalyst and fracture.

nodes.title: The Traitorous Eight (incl. Noyce, Moore, Hoerni…)
nodes.detail: Leave Shockley → Fairchild. Talent migration as the real West Coast invention.

nodes.title: Jean Hoerni
nodes.detail: Planar process — the manufacturing geometry that makes ICs sane.

nodes.title: Jack Kilby (TI)
nodes.detail: Integrated circuit demonstration — parallel invention geography in Texas.

nodes.title: Robert Noyce
nodes.detail: Planar IC interconnection path; later Intel co-founder.

nodes.title: Ted Hoff / Federico Faggin / Stan Mazor (and team)
nodes.detail: Intel 4004 era — microprocessor as a mapped product, not a single eureka.

blocks.heading: Invention map — devices that redraw edges

nodes.title: Point-contact transistor (1947)
nodes.detail: Proof that solid-state amplification works. Fragile, weird, world-changing.

nodes.title: Bipolar junction transistor
nodes.detail: More manufacturable family; radios and computers start to care.

nodes.title: Planar process
nodes.detail: Oxide, photolithography, batch fabrication — the map's industrial highway.

nodes.title: Integrated circuit
nodes.detail: Many devices, one chip. Kilby and Noyce paths converge commercially.

nodes.title: MOS / silicon-gate paths
nodes.detail: Density and power road toward LSI — the soil the microprocessor grows in.

nodes.title: First microprocessors (e.g. Intel 4004, 1971)
nodes.detail: CPU as a chip product. The map's destination for this page — not the end of semiconductors.

blocks.heading: Key edges (who/what connects)
rows: East Coast lab knowledge tries a West Coast company shape
Eight leave; Valley culture of spinout begins in earnest
Dallas node proves IC is not only a Bay story
Enough transistors in one package to be a CPU
blocks.caption: History as graph: labs spawn people; people carry process; process enables inventions; inventions fund new labs.

blocks.heading: Two geographies on the same map

columns.name: New Jersey / New York research belt
columns.detail: Bell Labs scale, wartime radar/communications inheritance, physics-first demonstration culture.

columns.name: Santa Clara Valley + Dallas production culture
columns.detail: Startup fission (Shockley→Fairchild→Intel) and TI's manufacturing muscle. Process and productization dominate.

blocks.heading: Walk the map in five stops

slides.title: Stop 1 — Murray Hill
slides.body: 1947: a point-contact oddity works. The lab is the hero; the device is still awkward.

slides.title: Stop 2 — Mountain View fracture
slides.body: Shockley's company concentrates talent, then loses it. The map gains a new company by subtraction.

slides.title: Stop 3 — Fairchild planar highway
slides.body: Hoerni's process turns transistors into a batchable geometry. ICs become a factory story.

slides.title: Stop 4 — Dallas parallel
slides.body: Kilby's IC shows the invention is bigger than one zip code.

slides.title: Stop 5 — Intel CPU chip
slides.body: Enough integration, and the computer's center of gravity moves onto silicon.

blocks.heading: Date anchors (not the narrative spine)
rows: Kilby IC; Noyce planar IC path
blocks.caption: Use dates to orient. Use the diagrams to understand causality.

blocks.quote: The transistor did not travel as a single invention. It traveled as people changing buildings, and buildings learning new processes.

blocks.title: Why not a pure timeline
blocks.body: A timeline suggests one lane of progress. The actual path is forked labs, parallel IC inventions, and alumni networks. This B page keeps the map primary on purpose.

blocks.heading: Map literacy
blocks.prompt: On this map, Fairchild matters most because it…
options: Concentrated planar manufacturing talent and spawned the Intel edge
Was the only lab that ever made transistors
Replaced Bell Labs as a government agency
blocks.explanation: Fairchild is the planar/IC talent hub and the alumni bridge to Intel — a relationship node, not just a date.

blocks.heading: Keep exploring
blocks.body: Pick one edge on the table and read a primary source about that hop — Shockley to Fairchild, or Fairchild to Intel. The map gets sharper every time you follow one line.
